The Story of Venerable Master Hsuan Hua's Leaving Home

Editor's note: The Venerable Hsuan Hua was a native of Shuangcheng county, Jilin province, of the Bai family. His father Fuhai was a farmer, thrifty all his life. His mother, née Hu, ate vegetarian and recited the Buddha's name every day of her life, loved giving and doing good—helping whoever needed help—so the village praised her as a living Bodhisattva. On the night of the 16th day of the 3rd lunar month in the Wuwu year, she dreamed that Amitabha Buddha descended, his body radiating light, illumining the world, shaking heaven and earth. Startling awake, she noticed a strange fragrance, wondrously sweet, filling her whole body, down into liver and lungs, bringing an inconceivable state. In a moment Duke Xuan was born, crying three days and three nights before stopping—as if already knowing the suffering beings must bear in this Saha world. Below are excerpted the Duke's own account of his leaving-home affinities.

As a child, before I turned twelve, I was a most stubborn child. How stubborn? If anyone teased me, I cried—and once crying, no one knew when I would stop. My parents' words did no good; I would not listen, doing only as I pleased. Often I refused food and drink, just wailing on—my parents gave up, helpless to make me obey. Then I knew my parents loved me dearly; seeing me refuse food, their hearts melted and they yielded to me. So unfilial was I then, heedless of my parents' suffering—thinking back now, I was truly rotten!

Once, a neighbor child came to play. Then I had just learned to crawl, and that child was also learning to crawl. We crawled on a platform, the two of us racing to see who crawled fastest. Seeing me crawl ahead of him, crawling behind, he bit my leg. What a fool I was! Instead of fighting back, I only knew how to cry. Remembering it now makes me laugh!

That year, when I was eleven, out playing with village children, I chanced to see the corpse of a small child. Never having seen such a sight since birth, I thought the child was sleeping—but calling, it would not wake; eyes closed, breath gone. Understanding nothing, home I asked my mother:

Why is that child sleeping out in the field? My mother said:

That child is dead.

Why must one die? I asked again.

- Why couldn't one die? My mother answered so.

Just then a relative said:

Only those who leave home to cultivate never die.

From then on, thinking of death I was afraid—I did not want to die. I felt living-then-dying was no good at all, and the thought of leaving home sprouted in my head—I wanted to cultivate to end birth and death.

One day I said to my mother:

- I wish to leave home to cultivate—I wonder if Mother approves?

My mother said:

- Leaving home is a fine thing—Mother cannot stop you. Yet Mother thinks: when Mother is gone, leaving home will still not be too late.

So my mother consented to my leaving home. I was overjoyed, though I could not yet go. At once I felt remorse for my past unfilial acts that had grieved my parents and taxed their hearts for me. How to repay such kindness? Thinking back and forth, I hit upon a way—a foolish way—bowing to my parents in repentance. Decided, I carried it out.

The moment I bowed down before my parents, they were most astonished, asking:

- What is this bowing about?

Because before I did unfilial things toward Father and Mother, angering you—now I know it was wrong, so from today I shall bow to Father and Mother.

My father said:

- Knowing your faults and repenting is good—no need to bow.

I replied:

I have always been stubborn—what I say, I must see through to the end.

My parents, knowing my nature well, said no more, letting me follow my wish—and so, morning and evening, they received my bows.

From that day, each morning at dawn, while the household still slept, I went to the yard and bowed three times to my father, three to my mother. Each night, after all had slept, I went to the yard again and bowed three times to each parent. After a while, feeling it not enough, I added bows to heaven and earth. Then I had never heard terms like king of heaven, king of earth, or king of men—knowing only heaven, earth, sovereign, father, mother, and teacher—so morning and evening I bowed three times to heaven, three to earth, three to the head of state, three to father, three to mother, three to my future teacher. Bowing so for a time, still feeling it not enough, I added bows to the greatly filial of the world, the greatly good of the world, the great worthies and great sages. Later I added bows to the good people of the whole world, as well as the not-good people of the world. Bowing to heaven, I prayed that great evildoers, the very worst, would reform from evil to good—all becoming good people.

The bows grew daily, reaching eight hundred and thirty (830) bows. Each session lasted two and a half hours, morning once, evening once—five hours a day in all. Whether gales blew or rains poured, I bowed the full count in the yard. Even in winter snow and rain, still in the yard. I also bowed to heaven praying for timely wind and rain, nation at peace, people secure.

Bowing so for several years, when my mother passed away I stayed by her grave, bowing on for three years. Afterward I left home and began studying the Sutra canon. I found Buddhist Sutras truly the richest, most complete treasury, which other religions lack—no canon compares.

Before leaving home, I had also joined other religions' activities—attending Protestant and Catholic services, even other Ways' Dharma assemblies—but on the whole, studying to the end to find the method ending birth and escaping death, it was truly disappointing, for those religions' doctrines never reach the ultimate. Yet people find Protestantism and Catholicism widely known and followed. Why? Because the New and Old Testaments are translated into many languages, their meaning simple and easy to grasp.

Buddhism's meaning, though perfect, has Sutra texts too lofty, beyond ordinary reach—so few follow it. So I vowed to translate the entire Tripitaka in twelve divisions into plain vernacular, then into every nation's tongue. A reckless vow—for I knew no foreign tongues, had no chance to learn them, lacked the wisdom to complete it—who knew if I could do it?

In 1962 I came to America to propagate the Buddhadharma. When affinities ripened, my disciples began translating to fulfill my vow. After years of effort, results are fairly fine, but the goal is still far—may everyone strive harder. Translating Sutras is sages' work—a supremely noble task. Rendering the whole Tripitaka in twelve divisions into English—no merit compares.

Today, a disciple has vowed to translate Buddhist Sutras into English, recalling my vow of years past. I hope my disciples will join hearts and forces to fulfill that vow.

Editor's note: At Nanhua Monastery, during his time with Venerable Hsu Yun, Duke Xuan was valued by Venerable Hsu Yun and appointed Dean of Studies of the Vinaya Academy, and shortly after Director of Education. At the precept-transmission ceremony Duke Xuan was appointed Witnessing Acharya. Later Duke Xuan received from Venerable Hsu Yun the transmission of the Guiyang lineage, becoming its 9th-generation Dharma heir.

On the road of propagating the Dharma, Venerable Hsuan Hua traveled from Hong Kong to America, where Duke Xuan lectured dozens of

Sutras, promoting all five schools—Chan, Teachings, Vinaya, Esoteric, Pure Land—tearing down the fences between schools, taking Buddhism's revival as his own duty, urging his disciples daily to investigate Chan, recite the Buddha's name, repent, study Sutras, and truly cultivate—upholding the Right Teaching, hoping the Right Dharma forever endures.

Venerable Hsuan Hua was born with transcendent wisdom and a marvelous memory—read once, remembered forever; lecturing Sutras or Dharma never from a prepared draft, but according to time and audience. With unobstructed eloquence, words flowing like water, everywhere the Way, meaning perfectly interfused—commanding all admiration.

Duke Xuan lecturing the Avatamsaka Sutra could close his eyes and recite the text, not a word wrong—a thing never seen. This writer saw with his own eyes, heard with his own ears—boundless admiration. His disciples were all educated university youth, each in awe before Duke Xuan's virtue and vast learning—all prostrating in full reverence.

At the Venerable's urging, young men and women—Chinese, American, Vietnamese—came seeking refuge and the Complete Precepts to leave home and cultivate. Among them were Ph.D.'s, master's and bachelor's graduates, daring to leave bright futures behind to enter the Buddha's gate seeking truth. Some practiced asceticism—fasting a week, or twenty-one days, thirty-six days, up to seventy-two days. Such asceticism is unprecedented in American Buddhist history—rare indeed through the ages. Others, praying for world peace, vowed the three-steps- one-bow pilgrimage, two years and six months unbroken, through wind and rain, offering their bodies as an example before the assembly. This happened precisely because the Venerable's transcendent virtue so moved them that they resolved to follow his self-forgetting, other-saving spirit in walking the Bodhisattva Way.

The Venerable teaches disciples methodically. Disciples keep the rules strictly, practice earnestly, always wearing the precept sash per the Buddha's rules, eating one meal daily at noon, sleeping without lying down. Nowhere in today's world is there another such place—so the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas may be called the world's Buddhist center, an inconceivable beacon for all Buddhist faithful.

In 1962 the Venerable brought the Right Dharma to the West, then founded the Dharma Realm Buddhist Association (its predecessor the Sino-American Buddhist Association), then the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas with branch Way-places in America, Canada, Taiwan, Malaysia. To train the world's pillar talent, at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas the Venerable established Dharma Realm Buddhist University, Instilling Virtue Secondary School, Nurturing Virtue Elementary School. For the Right Dharma's eternal endurance, uniting theory with practice, the Venerable further founded a program training Sangha and laity.

The Venerable also founded the International Translation Institute, aimed at spreading Buddhist Sutras worldwide. Today, a great many monks, nuns, and laity labor head-down translating Buddhist Sutras into English. To date, over a hundred Sutras and books in English and other Western tongues have been published and circulate.

The Venerable's devoted life is an offering to the Dharma, forgetting self. To this day, though the Dharma Realm Buddhist Association's branch Way-places scatter across America, Canada, and Asian countries, the Venerable ever keeps a humble, simple bearing, calling himself a "little ant," a lowly creature beneath all people, daring to contend with none. The Venerable once said:

"The City of Ten Thousand Buddhas is no private enterprise, but belongs to all Buddhist faithful of the world—even to faithful of all other religions worldwide. All now dwelling at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas labor devotedly, while I am only the gatekeeper—a cultivator of the Way, here awaiting those with affinities, come to cultivate together. Do not merely stand outside the gate. You are all members of the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas—in the future you will all become Buddhas."

Talks at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, Ten Thousand Buddhas Hall Chan Session, July 16 to 23, 1981.
